senses.gloss:
1. Candra, candra-mas, are the names of the ‘moon,’ the latter occurring from the Rigveda onwards, but the former being first used in this sense by the Atharvaveda. Very little is said about the moon in Vedic literature, except as identified with soma, both alike being described as waxing and waning. Reference is, however, made to the regular changes of the moon, and to its alternation with the sun, to which it, as soma, is declared in the Rigveda to be married. Mention is also made of its disappearance at the time of new moon, and of its birth from the light of the sun. In the Atharvaveda reference is made to demons eclipsing the moon (grahāś cāndramāsāḥ).
For the phases of the moon, and the month as a measure of time, see māsa. For the moon and its mansions, see nakṣatra.
^4) Rv. x. 55, 5. Cf. Av. x. 8, 32.

2. Candra appears to denote ‘gold’ in a certain number of passages from the Rigveda onwards.
Foot notes Rv. ii. 2, 4; iii. 31, 5; Av. xii. 2, 53; Jaittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 2, 7, 1; kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, ii. 6; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, iv. 26; xix. 93; pañcaviṃśa brāhmaṇa, vi. 6; Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, iii. 3, 3, 4, etc. Cf. the adjective candrin in Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xx. 37; xxxi. 31.

Cāndhanāyana is the patronymic of Ānandaja in the vaṃśa brāhmaṇa.
